title: Whose image? (Matthew 22:15–46)
hook: a coin with a face on it, and a question about whose face is on you
tomorrow: if Jesus said call no man father, why do some churches?

segments.voice: That was a week in Jerusalem: not so among you; that our eyes may be opened; out of the mouths of babes; he repented and went; the head of the corner. Yesterday's line: many called.

Pull a coin from a pocket or a jar and look: there's often a face on it. Here's yesterday's question. Some of Jesus' opponents bring him a trap. Is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar, or not? Say pay, and he sides with Rome. Say don't, and Rome hears it. He asks to see the coin. "Whose is this image and superscription?" Caesar's, they say. "Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's." They marvel, and leave.
screen: `A FACE ON A COIN.` → `A TRAP ABOUT TAXES.` → `WHOSE IS THIS IMAGE?`

segments.voice: Some readers hear something underneath. The coin carries Caesar's image, so give it back to him. What carries God's image? Genesis says God created man "in his own image." On that reading, the coin goes to Caesar, and the person holding it belongs to God. That verse is Jewish scripture first, and a teaching in the Mishnah draws a striking lesson from it: God began humankind with one person, so that no one could say to another, my ancestor was greater than yours. One image, one family. Then more questions come. To the lawyer who asks for the greatest commandment, Jesus answers from the Torah: love God with all your heart, soul and mind, and love your neighbor as yourself. "On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets." By the end, Matthew says, nobody dared ask him anything more.
screen: `RENDER UNTO CAESAR.` · `MADE IN HIS OWN IMAGE.` · `ONE ANCESTOR, SO NONE IS GREATER.` · `ON THESE TWO COMMANDMENTS.` · then, large: `RENDER UNTO GOD.`

segments.voice: Hold a coin, or any bill, and look at the face on it for a few breaths. Then set it down, turn your own hand over, and look at it the same way: the lines, the knuckles, the pulse at the wrist. In Genesis, that's where the other image is.
Whose image? Jesus' question over a coin: Caesar's face on the money, and, some readers add, God's on the one holding it.
Your line: render unto God, the things, and the people, that bear his image. Two weeks, done.
